sections.label: The opening
sections.line: October 2026: get hired for agentic work
sections.para: Agents are moving from pilots to products, and the tools and workflows are mature enough to glue together. As with breaking applications, building websites or mobile apps before, this skill now gets people hired, degree or not. Companies need AI operators, not model builders, the data shows employers prefer AI skills, and the edge starts with the application.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Operators wanted, and the edge starts early
sections.para: The first phase of agents has passed. Skills like web and mobile development once got people hired; this is that moment again. If you use email and apps well, you are technical enough. Companies need operators, not model builders. Employers say they prefer AI skills over experience, and when candidates look equal, the application decides.

sections.label: The moment
sections.line: From pilots to products, with a warning
sections.para: The tools and workflows are maturing, rough at the edges but usable together. Gartner predicted 40% of enterprise apps would have task-specific agents by 2026, and that over 40% of agentic projects will be cancelled by 2027. Together they place the bottleneck in people who can make agents useful and safe, so those on the outskirts should start now.

sections.label: There was a time
sections.line: Skills that got people hired, again and again
sections.para: Breaking applications, code review, threat modelling, decent programming without a degree, websites, email campaigns, mobile apps after the App Store opened in July 2008, Salesforce and spreadsheets: each got people hired on what they could show, then became normal. People who use all of these still say they are not technical; they are, and can learn the new techniques.

sections.label: Operators, not model builders
sections.para: The first wave of corporate AI hiring went to machine-learning specialists; LinkedIn's 2020 top emerging job was the AI specialist, defined by ML skills. Most companies needed operators instead: people who use the tools and workflows well. The nearest named role is the forward-deployed engineer, with postings up 1,165% year on year in 2025 by one analysis.

sections.label: What the data says
sections.para: In Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 survey, 66% of leaders would not hire someone without AI skills and 71% would rather hire a less experienced candidate with them. Only 39% of AI users had company training, so the skill is mostly self-taught. PwC's 2026 barometer found a 62% wage premium for AI skills, and those jobs growing about eight times faster.

sections.label: You have to do it to see it
sections.para: A group Dinis works with went from not building websites to building them easily with this workflow, and one of them now understands how the pieces fit. What changed their view was doing it, not an explanation. Explorer coding and the citizen developer make the same point: building what you need is how you learn the skill.

sections.label: When all things are equal
sections.para: However good you are, someone has to choose, and usually two or three candidates look equal against the job specification. Dinis's bet is that working with agentic workflows and being able to map a problem out gives a real edge, visible from the first step of the process.

sections.label: It starts with the application
sections.line: Bring something they have not seen
sections.para: Send a CV fitted to the role, an analysis of the company's problem, and something new: a graph, an infographic, a small site. Dinis got jobs through his OWASP work; in one interview he spent half the time helping them use his tool better. The interview started from his strengths, and agents now make that material cheap for every application.

sections.label: Where to start
sections.para: Pick one workflow and run it end to end, such as a voice memo turned into a checked article. Publish it, because linkable work can be shown. Use it in your next application: one analysis, one figure, one thing the employer has not seen.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.para: Working this way helps when the choice is close; it does not guarantee a job. AI operator is Dinis's term, not a surveyed title. Gartner's figures are forecasts and PwC's come from job adverts, not hires. The group mentioned is not named, and the change in them is an observation, not a measurement.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: A memo and the hiring data
sections.para: From Dinis's voice memo of 18 October 2026, with research that day: Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index, PwC's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer via its newswire release, Gartner's 2025 predictions, Bloomberry on forward-deployed engineers, LinkedIn's 2020 emerging jobs, Apple's 2008 App Store release, and his 2025 essay on presentations instead of CVs.
